name: Yara Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Yara. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government, and everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the motor claims team at a big national insurer, in the regional office by the train station, fourth floor. I get in at eight, open the queue and there are usually about forty car claims waiting: bumps in car parks, rear-end crashes, the odd write-off. I log the details, chase the police report if there is one, check the garage's repair estimate against our price list and phone the customer. I've done it six years, since I finished my college diploma.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people on the phone, honestly, even the angry ones, because most of them just had a horrible morning and want a human to say it'll be sorted. Bev, who sits next to me, has been there twenty years and we have lunch together every day. What wears me out is typing the same thing into three systems and the targets on the screen above our desks. Last spring they brought in a triage tool that sorts claims before we see them, and I just don't use the extra bits it offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I already say, which is that the triage tool is a fancy sorting hat and it still sends me claims in the wrong pile. Online I'd probably share a post saying the bosses oversold it. At work I'd tell Bev I told you so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it's a relief, but not a big one. Rent on our flat went up again in September and my pay rise didn't cover it. I've typed the same accident description into three different systems for six years, and nobody's ever offered to fix that for me. So even if AI does nothing, the job stays tiring and the money stays tight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my queue the way I do it now and keep ignoring the optional summary button. I'd go to the union meeting in January and ask our rep to get it written down that the triage tool won't be used to cut desks. Tomas and I would keep putting a bit aside, maybe 100 a month, which is what we manage now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, a bit irritated. It's not fear, it's more that nothing gets better either.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money stays tight. What's the pressure, exactly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent is the big one, it's nearly 40 percent of what we both bring home. Tomas is a bus mechanic at the city depot, so his pay is steady but not high. We've got about three months of savings, which sounds fine until the car needs a clutch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the triage tool quietly took a few routine claims off your desk, how would you notice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The queue would get shorter in the morning and then a manager would say we have capacity. That's the word they use before they don't replace someone. So even the small version makes me watch the empty chairs.

say: The triage tool is **oversold**, and it still sends claims to the **wrong pile**.
I'd tell my colleagues the managers **hyped it** to justify targets.
think: The relief is small, because **rent** already eats nearly **40 percent** of our pay.
Even small automation gives managers an excuse to leave **empty desks** unfilled.
do: Keep working the motor claims queue and **skip the optional** summary button.
Ask the **union rep** in January for a written promise of no desk cuts.
Keep saving about **100 a month** with Tomas, her partner.
feel: Steady but **irritated**, because nothing gets worse or **better**.
S0.quote: I've typed the same accident description into three different systems for six years, and nobody's ever offered to fix that for me.
fieldNote: Her worry here is **money**, not AI: rent rises outpace her pay rises.
She reads small changes through **staffing**: "capacity" means a chair stays empty.
She refuses tools on **principle**, not from confusion; she knows exactly what the button does.

steps.text: Keep working the motor claims queue without the optional summary tool
Ask the union rep for a written no-cuts promise in January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it straight: this is a company choosing shareholders over staff and calling it progress. I'd post about it in the union group chat and probably on my own page too. I wouldn't pretend it's the weather.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, my job is exactly the list on that card: checking, writing letters, answering customers. Motor claims would be one of the first teams they shrink. I think within two years our team of twelve goes to six, and I'm average, not the best, so I could be one of the six who go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's AI working group at the regional office straight away, so I'm in the room. Tomas and I would cut the holiday fund and put 200 a month into savings instead. I'd write to our local representative about rules for AI deciding claims, because someone should check the machine. I wouldn't start learning the tools; I'd rather fight for the people than train the thing that replaces them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tight in the chest. Angry, mainly, with a scared bit underneath I don't like admitting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bev, first. Twenty years on the team, she's 52 and she'd struggle to start somewhere new. When a desk goes empty on our floor, nobody says the word redundancy. They just move the plant over and spread the claims around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the tools. If learning them kept you in a job, would you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've thought about that, and I hate the question. Maybe, if it came to the rent or my pride, I'd do the minimum. But I'd still be in the union meeting every month making noise.

say: The company is choosing **shareholders over staff** and calling it progress.
I'd post in the **union group chat** and on my own page.
think: My work is exactly the list on the card: **checking, letters, customers**.
I expect our team of twelve to **halve**, and average clerks like me could go.
do: Join the union's **AI working group** at the regional office straight away.
Swap the holiday fund for **200 a month** in savings.
Write to the **local representative** about rules for AI deciding claims.
feel: **Angry** on top, with a **scared** feeling underneath she doesn't like admitting.
S1.quote: When a desk goes empty on our floor, nobody says the word redundancy. They just move the plant over and spread the claims around.
fieldNote: She immediately places her own team among the **first cut**, with no comfort.
Her loyalty runs to **colleagues** like Bev more than to the firm.
She admits she might **give in** and learn the tools if rent forced it.

steps.text: Join the union's AI working group at the regional office
Move 200 a month from the holiday fund into savings
Write to the local representative about AI deciding claims

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the biggest layoff in history and nobody voted for it. I'd go to every protest, honestly. Online I'd be the person nobody wants to sit next to at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm out of a job by 2028, maybe sooner, because claims is pure screen work. Tomas would have about three more years at the bus depot before robots can fix engines, so his pay would carry us for a while. Two years isn't time to plan anything. Two years is time to stop buying takeaway and hope the union gets us decent redundancy pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd cut everything: the gym, the streaming, the takeaway on Fridays, and we'd sell my little car and I'd take the bus. I'd push the union hard for a proper redundancy deal, at least a year's pay. Once it hit, I'd sign on for whatever government support exists and lean on Tomas's wage. I don't know what job I'd even retrain for when the robots are three years behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, really. Like the floor tilting. I'd be scared every time the office email pinged.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your mum about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum worked in a shoe factory that closed when I was ten, so she'd understand straight away. I'd tell my mum the same thing that happened to her factory is happening to my office, only faster. She'd probably say come home, and the worst part is I might have to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomas's job carries you for a while. What happens around 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's both of us, and that's the bit I can't picture. Three years of his wage is a bridge, not a home. I'd be hoping the government has figured something out by then, because we won't have.

say: This is the **biggest layoff** in history and nobody voted for it.
I'd go to **every protest** I could get to.
think: I expect to be **out of work** by 2028, because claims is pure screen work.
Tomas's bus depot job gives us roughly **three more years** before robots arrive.
do: Cancel the **gym, streaming** and Friday takeaway, and sell her small car.
Push the union for a **year's pay** in redundancy.
Sign on for **government support** and live on Tomas's wage once it hits.
feel: Sick and **scared**, like the floor **tilting** under her.
S2.quote: Two years isn't time to plan anything. Two years is time to stop buying takeaway and hope the union gets us decent redundancy pay.
fieldNote: She sees the three-year **robot gap** clearly, but only as Tomas's bridge, not hers.
Her mum's **factory closure** frames everything; this feels like a repeat.
She has no retraining idea at all; the **union deal** is her whole plan.

steps.text: Sell her small car and cancel the gym and streaming
Push the union for a full year's redundancy pay
Sign on for government support and live on Tomas's wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got five years, so there's no excuse for governments not to protect workers this time. I'd be pushing for rules now, while there's still time. At work I'd be telling people to join the union before it's too late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years doesn't save my job, it just makes the ending slower. Five years means I'd watch my job disappear one software update at a time, and I'd still be the one training the replacement. Tomas gets until about 2034, so we'd have a bit longer as a household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a union rep myself, probably next year, because someone has to bargain over how it's done. I'd save hard, 250 a month, so we'd have a year of rent by 2030. I'd vote for whoever promises a proper transition fund. Retraining, I don't know, I'd wait and see what jobs are left before I spend money on a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Less sick than the two-year one, more like a long dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see on retraining. What would make you move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I saw people from our office actually getting jobs somewhere after a course, I'd follow them. I'm not going to be the first one to jump. I've seen people spend 3,000 on courses that led nowhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would being a union rep cost you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Evenings, mostly, and probably a promotion I wasn't going to get anyway. Managers don't love reps. But I'd rather be the person who stood up than the one who kept quiet and got cut anyway.

say: Five years means governments have **no excuse** not to protect workers.
I'd tell colleagues to **join the union** before it's too late.
think: Five years doesn't save her job; it makes the **ending slower**.
She'd likely end up **training her replacement** one update at a time.
do: Stand as a **union rep** at the regional office next year.
Save **250 a month** to build a year of rent by 2030.
Vote for whoever promises a **transition fund** for displaced workers.
feel: A **long dread**, heavy rather than sick.
S3.quote: Five years means I'd watch my job disappear one software update at a time, and I'd still be the one training the replacement.
fieldNote: Extra time turns into **organising**, not personal escape.
She refuses to be the first to retrain, after seeing **3,000 courses** lead nowhere.
She still expects to **lose the job**; time only changes how she fights.

steps.text: Stand as union rep at the regional office next year
Save 250 a month towards a year of rent
Vote for a candidate promising a worker transition fund
Wait for colleagues' results before paying for any course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough time to do this decently, so let's actually do it decently. Pay people while they retrain, slow it down where it hurts. I'd still be loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years changes it for me. I'd be 37, still young enough to start over. Ten years is long enough to become someone else. I'd rather become a social worker than a person who checks what a machine already decided.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my claims job for now, but in two or three years I'd start a part-time social work course in the evenings. I'd keep saving 150 a month and stay in the union. I'd look at whether the course can be funded by the government, because I'm not paying full price on 3 months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calmer. Still worried, but it's the kind of worry you can do something with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why social work, of all things?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because on the phone the part I'm good at is the person, not the form. When someone's car is written off and they can't get their kid to school, I'm the one who calms them down. A machine can fill in a claim; I don't believe it can sit in someone's kitchen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're slow with new things. Does a course in your thirties scare you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It does, a lot. I failed my first year of maths at college and I still remember that feeling. But ten years gives me room to fail once and try again.

say: A decade is enough to do this **decently**, so governments should.
Pay people **while they retrain** and slow it where it hurts.
think: At **37** she'd still be young enough to start over.
She'd rather be a **social worker** than check a machine's decisions.
do: Keep the **claims job** for the next two or three years.
Start a part-time **social work course** in the evenings.
Look for **government funding** so she doesn't pay full price.
feel: **Calmer**, with a worry she can **act on**.
S4.quote: Ten years is long enough to become someone else. I'd rather become a social worker than a person who checks what a machine already decided.
fieldNote: Ten years is the first scenario where she imagines a **new self**.
She values the **human part** of her job and wants to keep only that.
Fear of failing a course, rooted in a **failed maths** year, still holds her back.

steps.text: Keep the motor claims job for two or three more years
Enrol in an evening part-time social work course
Keep saving 150 a month alongside Tomas
Stay a paying member of the staff union

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, easily, because there's no time and I've got no backup trade. I'm 27 and I've only ever known claims. If the claims go to a computer, I need somebody to tell me where a person like me goes next. What would help is real redundancy pay, a year at least, and paid retraining run by people who know what jobs actually exist.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Nobody on my floor will get a vote on any of this, and that's what makes me angriest. If workers had a say in how fast it came, I'd be a lot less scared.

headlineQuote: I'm 27 and I've only ever known claims. If the claims go to a computer, I need somebody to tell me where a person like me goes next.
portrait: Yara, 27, handles **motor claims** at a national insurer and rents a flat with Tomas, a bus mechanic.
She never uses AI tools and treats refusing them as a matter of **principle**.
Her answer to every scenario is the **union**: organise, bargain, push for rules.
Only with **ten years** does she picture a new career, in social work.
Her mum's **factory closure** shapes how she reads every warning.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she has no backup trade and only knows claims.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** run by people who know which jobs really exist.
